masthead.kicker: Hidden Champions of India / a DeepThought series

headline.text: Kesowa: a 15-person Kolkata drone-data startup with a real Coal India project on its record — and a revenue line that just fell by nearly 40%.

subhead.text: A DPIIT-recognized SaaS layer over drone-captured imagery, built by two of its three original founders after the third stepped away at incorporation — with two independently confirmed government clients and one specific, named coal-mine safety survey.
subhead.source: Zauba Corp; Tofler; IndiaFilings; The Company Check; SiliconIndia

snapshot.label: Funding
snapshot.value: Sardar Patel Tech. Business Incubator (terms undisclosed)

snapshot.label: Confirmed clients
snapshot.value: Kolkata Municipal Corp, WB Pollution Control Board, Eastern Coalfields (Coal India)

snapshot.value: Drone-data SaaS — not a drone manufacturer

p1_engine.eyebrow: A real but very small operation, with one substantiated flagship project and a steep recent revenue drop

blocks.text: Kesowa began as **Kesowa Infinite Ventures LLP** (LLPIN AAP-9584), founded **17 July 2019** in Kolkata by three co-founders — **Prayush Poddar** (CEO & CMO), **Vrint Poddar** (CTO), and **Vinayak Malhotra**. That LLP converted to the current entity, **Kesowa Infinite Ventures Private Limited** (CIN U31906WB2020PTC240808), on **24 October 2020**. Vinayak Malhotra does not appear as a director of the successor company, and his official director record (DIN 08512755) now shows only an unrelated current directorship — consistent with him stepping back around the conversion rather than continuing with the business.
blocks.source: Zauba Corp; Tofler; IndiaFilings (LLP and DIN records)

blocks.text: Revenue was **₹46.72 lakh in FY2025, down 39% year-on-year** — a steep drop, not a minor softening. No cause was independently confirmed despite a direct search; this is a first-party question (e.g. whether a specific government project completed without a replacement contract yet lined up) that only the founders can really answer. The company runs on a very small base: ~14-16 employees, ₹5 lakh paid-up capital, recognized as a DPIIT (Startup India) startup. It has drawn investment from the **Sardar Patel Technology Business Incubator** (a Mumbai-based accelerator with 89 portfolio investments), though the specific amount and date weren't independently findable.
blocks.source: The Company Check (FY25 revenue and YoY change); direct research (incubator terms not publicly findable)

blocks.text: Kesowa's actual business is a **drone-data SaaS/analytics layer, not drone manufacturing** — MCA classifies its activity as "IT consulting and support services." Its two main products are the **Drone Call Center** (an on-demand aerial-intelligence platform, claiming "20x higher resolution" imagery) and **ARU Skynet/ARU Server** (drone-data management software with AI features including a Tree Count AI model and a Visual Pollution Index). These technical claims are self-published, with no independent benchmark or patent filing found to substantiate them. Whether Kesowa itself operates/pilots drones, or works entirely through third-party pilots processing imagery through its software, was not established despite a direct search.
blocks.source: MCA; company site (self-reported); direct research (unresolved operating model)

blocks.text: **The most credible evidence in this profile is a specific, named government/PSU project.** Kesowa completed a drone survey for Eastern Coalfields Limited (ECL), a real Coal India subsidiary, assessing haul-road and slope safety at its open-cast mine in Kalipahari, West Bengal, after the site had experienced heavy rain — producing a 3D model in place of a slower, more dangerous manual survey. That level of specific, checkable detail (named subsidiary, named location, a specific triggering event) is meaningfully stronger than a bare client-logo claim, even though it's still Kesowa's own published case study rather than independent press. Separately, an independent press source corroborates real project work with Kolkata Municipal Corporation and the West Bengal Pollution Control Board specifically. The remaining nine names on Kesowa's client list (including NKDA, Maharashtra Labour Welfare Board, Tamil Nadu, Nagpur Municipal Corporation, CESC, and others) are self-claimed only.
blocks.source: Kesowa's own ECL case study; SiliconIndia

p2_market.eyebrow: A fast-growing, policy-supported market — dominated in the public narrative by hardware makers Kesowa isn't one of

insights.point: India's drone market is **growing at a healthy pace, with real government policy behind it.**
insights.evidence: $1.32 billion (2025) heading to $2.73 billion by 2034, an 8.45% CAGR (one source; a second puts 2024 at $1.58B — broadly consistent magnitude). A proposed PLI 2.0 scheme (~₹1,000 crore) targets 30% local drone production, on top of an existing ₹120 crore PLI allocation.

insights.point: But the market's loudest names are **playing a different game entirely.**
insights.evidence: ideaForge, Garuda Aerospace, and Asteria Aerospace — the most-cited players — are drone HARDWARE manufacturers (ideaForge alone won ~₹100 crore in additional defense procurement in a single month, Nov 2025). Kesowa doesn't build drones; it builds software that analyzes what drones capture. These aren't real competitors so much as a different business entirely wearing the same industry label.
insights.source: company/press sources on ideaForge, Garuda Aerospace, Asteria Aerospace

insights.point: The closer comparison is a company most market write-ups don't lead with.
insights.evidence: Skylark Drones — a drone-data-and-analytics services company, not a hardware maker — is the more meaningful peer for Kesowa's actual business model, even though it isn't independently sized here.

insights.point: Government and PSU procurement is a **real, if narrow, demand channel** — and it's the one Kesowa has actually broken into.
insights.evidence: Municipal corporations, pollution control boards, and coal-mining PSUs represent a recurring, tender-driven demand source distinct from the defense/consumer segments the bigger hardware names chase.

reflect.text: Kesowa is a genuinely tiny player — 14-16 people, under ₹50 lakh in revenue — inside a market whose public narrative is dominated by much larger hardware companies it doesn't actually compete with. Its real foothold is narrower and more specific: a small number of real government and PSU relationships, won project by project, in a market segment (drone-data services, not drone manufacturing) that gets less attention than the hardware story but is arguably the more honest description of what Kesowa actually does.

p2_market.sourceNote: Market data: IMARC Group, Custom Market Insights, Nexdigm, MarketsandMarkets. Peer research: company/press sources on Skylark Drones, ideaForge, Garuda Aerospace, Asteria Aerospace.

p3_opportunities.lede: Four places worth a closer look, each built on something Kesowa already has or a gap already visible in its own numbers.

items.title: Diagnose the 39% revenue drop directly
items.body: A drop this steep isn't self-explanatory. Pinning down whether a completed government project simply hasn't been replaced yet, or whether something more structural is at play, is the single most urgent open question here.
items.source: The Company Check (FY25 revenue and YoY change)

items.title: Turn the ECL project into independently verifiable proof
items.body: The Eastern Coalfields case study is specific and credible, but it's still self-published. A named testimonial, a joint press mention, or an ECL/Coal India acknowledgment would convert a strong internal case study into external proof the next government tender committee can independently check.
items.source: Kesowa's own ECL case study; SiliconIndia

items.title: Substantiate the technical claims
items.body: "20x higher resolution" and the Tree Count AI / Visual Pollution Index models are currently marketing language with no independent benchmark or patent behind them. Even a basic published accuracy metric, or a first patent filing, would give these claims real weight in a competitive tender.

items.title: Clarify and formalize the drone-operations model
items.body: Whether Kesowa flies its own drones or works through partner pilots wasn't established here, and it's not a small detail — it changes the pitch, the regulatory footprint (DGCA relevance), and how scalable the business actually is. Settling this internally, then stating it plainly to clients, removes an ambiguity a careful government buyer would eventually ask about anyway.

guesslabel.text: Possibilities, not prescriptions. Which would work, and how much, only Kesowa's own data and people can tell. Each is small, made to learn fast.

items.title: Map FY25 revenue against the project calendar
items.body: Lay FY24 and FY25 revenue against a timeline of which government/PSU projects started and ended in each period — this alone would likely show whether the decline is a timing gap or something else.

items.title: Request one written reference from ECL/Coal India
items.body: A single short, quotable reference or letter of appreciation from the Eastern Coalfields project would upgrade the strongest case study in the portfolio from self-published to independently attributable.

items.title: Publish one accuracy metric for the Tree Count AI model
items.body: Pick the most mature AI feature and publish a simple, honest accuracy comparison against manual counting on one real project — a concrete number beats a resolution-multiplier claim in a technical evaluation.

items.title: Write one clear paragraph on the operating model
items.body: State plainly, in one place, whether Kesowa's own team flies the drones or partners with licensed operators — removing the ambiguity before a prospective government client has to ask.

takeaway.text: Kesowa's realest asset isn't its software feature list — it's a small number of genuine, specific government and PSU relationships, including a documented coal-mine safety survey most companies its size would never win. **The 39% revenue drop is the number that matters most right now**, and it isn't explained by anything public. Everything else here — the AI-model claims, the founding-team reshuffle, the funding — is smaller than that one open question.
